summary: Specifies an RTP payload header format for carrying video streams produced under the 1998 version of ITU-T Recommendation H.263. It lets this video be sent in real time over IP networks. It was a proposed standard, replaced by RFC 4629.

eli5.summary: Video is chopped into small pieces to travel over the internet. This says exactly how to label and pack the pieces of one video format so the receiver can put them back together.

subtitle: How to send 1998 ITU-T H.263 video over real-time IP networks

tldr.problem: Video compressed with the 1998 ITU-T Recommendation H.263 (H.263+) must be sent over IP networks in real time. The video codec produces a bitstream, but there is no standard way to split it into network packets, align it with the RTP protocol, and ensure the receiver can reassemble it and recover from packet loss.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2429 defines an RTP payload header format for H.263+ video. It specifies how to encapsulate H.263+ bitstreams in RTP packets, how to handle picture start codes, how to attach picture header copies for error resilience, and how to use Video Redundancy Coding (multiple independent streams) to allow recovery from packet loss.
tldr.outcome: H.263+ video can be reliably transmitted over IP networks. The RFC was later updated by RFC 4629 to account for changes in the video codec and network conditions.

facts.label: Start code omission
facts.value: First 2 zero bytes replaced by P bit

today: RFC 2429 specified RTP payload format for H.263+ video. It was later superseded by RFC 4629, which consolidated the H.263+ and H.263 payload formats and improved the specification based on implementation experience.

sections.title: H.263+ Video and Its Challenge
sections.content:
The H.263+ video codec is defined by the 1998 version of ITU-T Recommendation H.263. It improves on the 1996 version with new coding options that provide better compression, error resilience, and flexibility. Key new features include:

  • Slice structured mode: Pictures can be divided into slices at macroblock boundaries, allowing better packetization and error isolation.
  • Independent segment decoding (ISD): Video segments are encoded so that each is independently decodable, preventing errors in one segment from affecting others.
  • Reference picture selection: The encoder can choose an older reference frame (not just the most recent one) for prediction, allowing recovery from past frame loss.
  • Scalability: Temporal (frame-rate), SNR (quality), and spatial (resolution) scalability are supported, allowing layered transmission.

When an H.263+ encoder produces a video bitstream, that bitstream must be transported over IP networks in real time using RTP. However, the raw bitstream cannot simply be dropped into packets. It must be carefully packetized to handle network constraints like maximum packet size and packet loss, while preserving the timing and structure of the video data. RFC 2429 specifies exactly how to do this.
sections.eli5: H.263+ is a way to squeeze video down to a small size. To send it over the internet as packets, you need rules about how to cut it and label each piece so the other side knows how to put it back together.

sections.title: Payload Header and Packet Structure
sections.content:
Each RTP packet carrying H.263+ video has three layers: the RTP fixed header, a variable-length H.263+ payload header, and the compressed video bitstream.

The RTP header marks important fields for H.263+: the Marker bit is set to 1 when a packet contains the end of a frame (and 0 otherwise). The Payload Type specifies H.263+ video. The RTP Timestamp uses a 90 kHz clock (the same as H.261) and must be synchronized with the temporal reference in the H.263+ picture header.

The H.263+ payload header is variable-length, always at least 16 bits. It contains:

  • RR (5 bits): Reserved, must be zero.
  • P (1 bit): Set to 1 if the packet starts at a Picture, GOB (Group of Blocks), Slice, EOS (End of Sequence), or EOSBS (End of Bitstream) start code. This allows omitting the leading zero bytes of the start code, saving space.
  • V (1 bit): Set to 1 if an 8-bit Video Redundancy Coding (VRC) extension follows.
  • PLEN (6 bits): Length in bytes of an attached picture header copy (0 if none).
  • PEBIT (3 bits): Number of bits to ignore in the last byte of the attached picture header.
sections.eli5: Each packet has a label (the payload header) that tells the receiver important things: does this packet start a new picture? Is there error-correction data? How many bytes is the extra picture information? This label is typically 16 bits, but can be longer.

sections.title: Packetization and Error Resilience
sections.content:
Picture segment packets (P=1) start at a Picture, GOB, or Slice start code. The first two zero bytes of the start code are omitted from the bitstream and instead represented by setting P=1. Optionally, if the packet starts with an abbreviated picture header (incomplete UFEP), a complete picture header can be attached in the payload header (PLEN>0) to provide error resilience. If the original picture header is lost in transit, the receiver can use this redundant copy.

Continuation packets (P=0) carry bitstream data that does not start at a segment boundary. They are used when a single segment does not fit in one packet, or when other synchronization points are not available.

Picture start codes begin new frames. When the first packet of a frame contains only the picture start code (PSC), PLEN is normally 0, meaning no extra picture header is attached. However, if the bitstream uses an incomplete picture header (for compression), a complete copy can be attached for resilience.

Sequence ending packets (also P=1) mark the end of a video sequence with an EOS or EOSBS code. They have P=1 and PLEN=0 always.
sections.eli5: Packets have two types: some start a new picture or segment (marked with P=1), and others are just continuation of the same segment (P=0). To protect against lost packets, you can attach a spare copy of the picture setup information so the receiver can still decode even if the original copy never arrived.

sections.title: Video Redundancy Coding for Packet Loss
sections.content:
Video Redundancy Coding (VRC) is an optional mechanism to improve resilience when packets are lost. It works by transmitting multiple independent threads of video, each with its own reference frame chain.

In traditional video coding, each frame is predicted from the previous frame. If that previous frame is lost, the current frame and all subsequent frames become undecodable. VRC sends multiple independently-predicted threads. If one thread's frame is lost, the other threads are unaffected, allowing later frames to still be decoded.

All threads periodically converge at a sync frame (an intra-coded picture), which is sent redundantly in multiple threads. Between sync frames, each thread maintains its own prediction chain. When packet loss occurs in one thread, you can switch to another thread at the next sync frame.

The VRC header extension (8 bits, indicated by V=1) contains:

  • TID (3 bits): Thread ID (0-7). Thread 0 is the canonical thread.
  • Trun (4 bits): Monotonically increasing packet counter within the thread (modulo 16).
  • S (1 bit): Set to 1 if the packet contains a sync frame.

By observing the Trun counter and the RTP sequence number, a transport layer can determine if packets have been lost within a thread and handle packet reception priorities appropriately.
sections.eli5: Instead of sending one copy of each picture, you can send multiple versions, each following a different path through previous pictures. If one version is lost, you still have the others. Every so often, all versions show the same picture so they can resynchronize.

sections.title: Timing and Scalability Considerations
sections.content:
H.263+ supports a frame clock frequency expressed as 1800000/(cd*cf) pictures per second, where cd is 1-127 and cf is 1000 or 1001. Using the 90 kHz RTP clock, the time increment between H.263+ pictures must be an integer multiple of (cd*cf)/20. This ensures proper synchronization between the RTP timestamp and the H.263+ temporal reference (TR).

For common frame rates, the time increments are exact multiples: 3003 for 29.97 Hz NTSC, 3600 for 25 Hz PAL, 3750 for 24 Hz film, and 1500, 1250, or 1200 for 60, 72, or 75 Hz display rates. Custom frame rates may require mathematical rounding.

In temporal scalability scenarios, bi-directionally predicted frames (B-frames) are disposable. Because B-frames depend on future frames, they can be dropped without affecting the decoding of other frames. RTP timestamps for B-frames may not be monotonically increasing.

In spatial and SNR scalability scenarios, each enhancement layer is transmitted to a different IP address and port. All layers corresponding to the same temporal reference use the same RTP timestamp for proper synchronization. The configuration of layer numbers (ELNUM, RLNUM) and scalability type must be determined at session start and remain fixed.
sections.eli5: Video timing must be exact so the receiver plays it at the right speed. Some pictures can be thrown away without breaking playback. High-quality versions can be sent separately and reassembled if bandwidth allows.
